title: Systematic review: exercise-induced gastrointestinal syndrome - implications for health and intestinal disease
authors: Costa RJS, Snipe RMJ, Kitic CM, Gibson PR
population: Healthy populations and those with chronic GI conditions in studies of acute exercise (injury, permeability, endotoxaemia, motility, malabsorption)
findings: With increasing exercise intensity and duration, intestinal injury, permeability and endotoxaemia increase, with impaired gastric emptying, slower small-intestinal transit and malabsorption.
Heat stress and running mode appear to exacerbate these markers.
Exercise stress of >= 2 h at 60% VO2max appears to be the threshold for significant GI perturbations, irrespective of fitness status.

GI symptoms (upper and lower) are common and a limiting factor in prolonged strenuous exercise; effects are reversible in healthy populations; safety of strenuous exercise in chronic GI disease has not been established.
limitations: Heterogeneous markers and protocols; most studies shorter than ultras; no performance dose-response.
implications: Hot-weather rule: when forecast heat is high, reduce intensity and expectations of GI tolerance for long runs.
Treat sessions of >= 2 h at ~60% VO2max-equivalent effort as the point where fuelling practice becomes relevant to GI adaptation.
Medical disclaimer for athletes with known GI disease; do not prescribe high-CHO strategies to them.

verification.notes: Crossref match (dash/hyphen formatting only); findings confirmed in the Europe PMC abstract.
